295.title: Patanjali falls into open hands
295.hook: a small snake falls into a woman's prayer, and the book he brings begins with 'now'
295.carry: atha: the student is here, the teaching begins
295.tomorrow: what does Patanjali say yoga actually is?
295.howItsDone: The Yoga Sutras are studied line by line with a teacher and a commentary, often chanted in Sanskrit first; many yoga classes in the tradition open with a Sanskrit invocation bowing to Patanjali with folded hands before the teaching begins.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shatpadi, the hymn that closed Dvaita and beyond: the wave belongs to the ocean, never the ocean to the wave. svatantra: only God is independent. Today, a new week, a new teacher, and a story about how he arrived.

A woman named Gonika stands in a river at dawn, her palms cupped full of water, ready to offer it to the sun. She prays for a student, someone to pass on what she knows. Far above, the story goes, Adishesha, the great serpent Vishnu rests on, has asked to go down to earth and teach. He looks down, sees her open hands, and drops in, as a tiny snake. Then he takes the form of a child. She names him for how he came: pata, fallen, into anjali, cupped hands. Patanjali.
screen: `A WOMAN AT DAWN, HANDS CUPPED.` → `A SMALL SNAKE FALLS IN.` → `PATA + ANJALI: PATANJALI.`

segments.voice: That's a story many yoga schools tell, not history. Nobody knows much about the real Patanjali, and scholars' guesses for his date span several centuries. But the story says something on purpose: the teacher comes from Vishnu's own couch, and he lands where someone is ready, hands open. His book is the Yoga Sutras. A sutra is a thread: a short line, packed tight, meant to be memorized and unpacked by a teacher. It's the root text of Yoga, one of the six classical schools of Hindu philosophy, and here yoga isn't a workout. It's a path for the mind, toward freedom. The first thread is atha yoga anushasanam: now, the teaching of yoga. Atha is how many Sanskrit books begin, and it's counted an auspicious sound. The classic commentary, traditionally credited to Vyasa, reads it simply: here the subject starts. Many teachers hear more in it: the preparation is over, the student has arrived, the teaching can begin. Many yoga classes still open with a Sanskrit verse to Patanjali: for yoga that clears the mind, grammar that clears speech, and medicine that clears the body, I bow to him with folded hands. Folded hands. Anjali again. He came into cupped palms, and students still meet him that way.
screen: `A STORY, NOT HISTORY.` · `A SUTRA IS A THREAD.` · `YOGA: ONE OF SIX CLASSICAL HINDU SCHOOLS.` · `ATHA: NOW, THE TEACHING BEGINS.` · `I BOW WITH FOLDED HANDS.` · then, large: `ATHA YOGĀNUŚĀSANAM.`

segments.voice: Sit as you are and rest your hands in your lap, cupped and open, the way Gonika held the water. Notice what's here: the nearest sound, your breath, the mood you came in with. Whenever your mind leaves for later or earlier, say the word gently, atha, now, and come back with open hands. At the end, if you pray, fold your hands and bow, to God or to the teachers who brought this to you; if you don't, a small bow of thanks works too.
Atha, now. The first thread of the Yoga Sutras is atha yoga anushasanam: now, the teaching of yoga. The teaching begins when the student arrives, hands open.
Your line: atha, the student is here, the teaching begins. Patanjali fell into open hands. Day two ninety-five.

296.title: Vivekananda's drunk monkey
296.hook: a monk in New York tells Americans their mind is a drunk monkey, then defines yoga
296.carry: yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings
296.tomorrow: when the lake goes still, who is looking?
296.howItsDone: Students of the Yoga Sutras often memorize 1.2 in Sanskrit, and many yoga teachers in India and abroad quote it as the definition of yoga before teaching any posture.

segments.voice: Yesterday, atha, now: Patanjali fell into open hands, and his book opens the teaching for someone who has arrived.

New York, 1895. A young monk from Calcutta, Swami Vivekananda, has taken rooms in the city and is teaching small classes to Americans who have barely heard the word yoga. He doesn't start with poses. He tells them about a monkey. A monkey is restless by nature. Now someone gives it wine, so it's drunk. Then a scorpion stings it. Then a demon gets into it. That, he says, is the human mind: drunk on desire, stung by jealousy, seized by pride. And the line he keeps coming back to is Patanjali's second.
screen: `NEW YORK, 1895.` → `A RESTLESS MONKEY.` → `DRUNK, STUNG, POSSESSED.` → `THAT'S THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Here it is: yogash chitta vritti nirodhah. Yoga is the stilling of the turnings of the mind. Chitta is the mind in the widest sense: thinking, feeling, remembering. Vritti means a turning, a whirl, from a root that means to turn, like a wheel: the thoughts, the moods, the commentary that never stops. Nirodha means stilling, restraining, bringing to rest. Four words, and not one is about the body. That's the heart of yoga as a Hindu teaching: it's a discipline of the mind. Posture gets only a few threads in the whole book, and most poses taught in classes today grew up much later. Vivekananda gave his students a second picture, a lake. When wind ripples it, you can't see the bottom. When the water goes still, you see all the way down. Why would a Hindu want to see the bottom? Because of what's under the ripples. Patanjali calls it the seer; the Upanishads call it atman, the self. Nirodha can be read as restraint, even cessation, but many teachers hear it as a settling, water going still, not a lid slammed down. And the drunk monkey isn't hopeless. Vivekananda's advice: don't fight it. Let it jump, and watch. Day by day, he said, it gets calmer.
screen: `YOGAŚ CITTA-VṚTTI-NIRODHAḤ.` · `CHITTA, VRITTI, NIRODHA: MIND, TURNING, STILL.` · `NOT ONE WORD ABOUT THE BODY.` · `A LAKE WITH NO WIND.` · `UNDER THE RIPPLES: THE SEER.` · then, large: `YOGA IS THE STILLING OF THE MIND'S TURNINGS.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the monkey jump: don't chase it and don't scold it, just watch where it goes, a text, a sound, a small worry. Picture each one as wind on a lake, crossing the surface and passing, and when the water is flat for a moment between them, rest there. If you pray, you can let that stillness be your prayer; if you don't, let it simply be quiet.
Vritti, a turning of the mind. Yoga is the stilling of these turnings: chitta, vritti, nirodha. Mind, turning, stillness.
Your line: yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings. Not your toes. The monkey. Day two ninety-six.

297.title: Two birds on one tree
297.hook: one bird eats the fruit, one bird only watches; when the lake goes still, who is looking?
297.carry: you are the seer, not your weather
297.tomorrow: five kinds of thought, and one of them is sleep?
297.howItsDone: In classical yoga study, sutras 1.3 and 1.4 are read with the Samkhya distinction between purusha, the seer, and prakriti, the seen, and meditation is described as learning to witness the mind rather than be swept along by it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vritti: yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings. A drunk monkey, and a lake going still.

Two birds, close friends, sit on the same tree. One hops from branch to branch eating the fruit, sweet ones, bitter ones, and every bite changes its mood. A sweet one, and it's thrilled. A bitter one, and it's miserable. The other bird eats nothing. It just watches, calm. Then, now and then, the eating bird, sick of the bitter fruit, looks up and sees its friend, and its sorrow falls away. That's a picture from the Upanishads, and Hindus have handed it down for thousands of years.
screen: `TWO BIRDS, ONE TREE.` → `ONE EATS, SWEET AND BITTER.` → `ONE ONLY WATCHES.` → `THE EATER LOOKS UP.`

segments.voice: Patanjali's next two threads say it in yoga's language. Thread three: tada drashtuh svarupe avasthanam. Then, when the turnings are still, the seer rests in its own nature. Drashta, the seer, the one who sees. Thread four says what happens otherwise: the seer takes the shape of the turnings. The anger arrives, and you become angry. Teachers use a crystal: set a clear crystal by a red flower and it looks red. It never was. This is one of Hinduism's big teachings: you are not your thoughts. Patanjali, leaning on the related Samkhya school, calls the seer purusha, pure awareness, and puts the body and even the mind on the other side, among the things seen. The Upanishads call what's underneath atman, the self, and many teachers call it the sakshi, the witness. The schools describe it differently. In the Upanishad, the watching bird is usually read as the Lord, or the highest self; yoga teachers often borrow it for the seer. Either way the move is the same: the eating bird looks up. A feeling can be fully there, sweet or bitter, while something in you sees it. That's why many Hindu teachers describe meditation as learning to witness.
screen: `TADĀ DRAṢṬUḤ SVARŪPE 'VASTHĀNAM.` · `A CRYSTAL NEXT TO A RED FLOWER.` · `YOU ARE NOT YOUR THOUGHTS.` · `ATMAN. THE WITNESS.` · then, large: `YOU ARE NOT YOUR WEATHER.`

segments.voice: Let a thought come, any thought, and instead of following it, notice it the way the quiet bird watches the other one eat. Each time, step back half a step: there's the thought, and here is the one seeing it; you don't have to name the seer, just notice that seeing is happening. If you pray, you can rest in that quiet as a prayer, in the company of the Lord; if you don't, simply rest in the watching.
Drashta, the seer, the one who sees. When the turnings still, the seer rests in its own nature. Otherwise it takes the shape of its thoughts, like the bird lost in the fruit.
Your line: you are the seer, not your weather. Two birds, one tree. Day two ninety-seven, done.

298.title: Indra asks what the self is
298.hook: a god goes back to his teacher four times, and the last answer is about deep sleep
298.carry: even in deep sleep, the self is there
298.tomorrow: Arjuna says the mind is like the wind. what does Krishna say?
298.howItsDone: Students of the Yoga Sutras often learn the five vrittis as a list and use them in meditation, noting which kind of thought is arising rather than following it; Hindu teachers often pair the list with the Upanishads' teaching that the self is the witness of waking, dream and deep sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday, drashta, the seer: two birds on one tree, one eating, one watching. You are not your weather.

A god and a demon walk up to the same teacher. Indra, king of the gods, and Virochana, a prince of the asuras, both want one thing: to know the self. The teacher, Prajapati, has them live with him thirty-two years. Then he says: dress in your finest, and look into a pan of water. What you see, that's the self. Virochana sees his own body, all dressed up, and goes home delighted: the self is the body. Indra gets halfway home and stops. If the self is the body, it dies with the body. So he goes back.
screen: `A GOD AND A DEMON ASK THE SAME QUESTION.` → `LOOK IN THE WATER.` → `VIROCHANA: THE SELF IS THE BODY.` → `INDRA GOES BACK.`

segments.voice: Thirty-two more years, and Prajapati says: the one who moves about in dreams, that's the self. Indra stops again. In dreams you can still be chased, still weep. Back he goes. Thirty-two more: the one in deep, dreamless sleep, that's the self. And Indra: but then you know nothing at all, not even I am. Five more years, and at last Prajapati tells him: the body is mortal, but it's the home of the self, which isn't; the self is the one who knows. A hundred and one years of asking. Patanjali takes deep sleep seriously too. Thread six sorts every turning of the mind into five kinds: right knowing; error, like the rope at dusk you take for a snake; imagination, words with nothing real behind them; sleep; and memory. Why is sleep on the list? The commentary's answer: you wake up and say, I slept well. Something was there to know it. Put the two together, the way many Vedanta teachers do, and you have a big Hindu teaching about the atman, the self: it isn't the body, or the dream, or the blank of deep sleep. It's the one who is there through all three. Teachers also use the five drawers in meditation. A worry at two in the morning is often imagination, not knowing. Name the drawer, and it loosens.
screen: `THE DREAMER? INDRA GOES BACK.` · `DEEP SLEEP? INDRA GOES BACK.` · `101 YEARS OF ASKING.` · `PRAMĀṆA-VIPARYAYA-VIKALPA-NIDRĀ-SMṚTAYAḤ.` · `I SLEPT WELL: SOMETHING KNEW.` · then, large: `THE SELF IS THERE THROUGH ALL THREE.`

segments.voice: Let the mind do what it does, and when a thought comes, give it a drawer, softly: memory, imagination, knowing, error, or even sleep if you drift toward drowsiness. You don't need to be right about the drawer; label it, let it go, and notice the one who is noticing, the way Indra kept asking who that was. If you pray, you can rest in that quiet with God; if not, simply rest.
Nidra, sleep, one of the five turnings of the mind. You wake and say, I slept well, and Hindu teachers say: then something was there.
Your line: even in deep sleep, the self is there. Indra asked for a hundred and one years to learn it. See you tomorrow.

segments.voice: My mind is restless. Holding it still is like holding the wind. That's Arjuna in the Gita, more or less, a few months ago on this path, stopping Krishna somewhere in the sixth chapter. Anyone who has tried to meditate for five minutes knows the feeling. Krishna doesn't argue. He agrees: yes, the mind is hard to hold. Then he gives two words for how it's done. Patanjali, in thread twelve, gives the very same two.
screen: `ARJUNA: MY MIND IS LIKE THE WIND.` → `KRISHNA AGREES.` → `TWO WORDS.`

segments.voice: Thread twelve: abhyasa vairagyabhyam tan nirodhah. By practice and non-attachment, they are stilled; they, meaning the turnings. Two words carry the whole method. Abhyasa, practice: coming back, again and again, to the thing you've chosen. Vairagya, non-attachment: letting go of the pull. Literally it means without coloring, without the red flower staining the crystal. Teachers often say the two are like the two wings of a bird. One wing alone, and you fly in circles. Practice without letting go becomes grinding: you sit every day, jaw clenched, demanding results. Letting go without practice becomes drifting: you're very relaxed and nothing changes. Coming back, and not clutching. And here is the Gita's answer to Arjuna, in that sixth chapter: the mind is restless, hard to hold, but it can be held by practice and by dispassion. The same pair, in the same order. Two great texts, from different schools, agree on the method. Now make it small, the way Hindus do it. Practice is the next bead on a mala, the name said again each time the mind runs off. Letting go is not needing that sitting to feel special, and not keeping score. Tomorrow and the day after, Patanjali takes each wing on its own.

300.title: Dhruva, the star that never moves
300.hook: a five-year-old is pulled off his father's lap, and practices until he becomes the pole star
300.carry: abhyasa: long, steady, with care, becomes firm ground
300.tomorrow: Death offers a boy gold, horses and heaven. what does he say?
300.howItsDone: Many Hindus keep a daily sadhana, often japa, repeating a name of God on a mala of 108 beads; children hear Dhruva's story as the boy whose steady devotion made him the pole star, and teachers of the Yoga Sutras cite 1.14 to explain why steadiness matters more than intensity.

segments.voice: Day three hundred. Yesterday, abhyasa and vairagya: practice, and let go, two wings of one bird. Today, the first wing, and a boy who practiced until he became a star.

A small prince, Dhruva, five years old in most tellings, climbs onto his father's lap. His stepmother pulls him off. That seat isn't for you, she says. If you want it, go pray to Vishnu to be born again as my son. Dhruva runs to his mother in tears. She doesn't tell him to fight back. She tells him: then go to Vishnu. So a little boy walks out of the city toward the forest. On the way, the sage Narada meets him and gives him a practice: a place to sit, and a name to repeat. Om namo bhagavate vasudevaya.
screen: `PULLED OFF HIS FATHER'S LAP.` → `THEN GO TO VISHNU.` → `NARADA GIVES HIM A NAME.`

segments.voice: Dhruva sits by the river Yamuna and practices. The Bhagavata counts it out, month by month: fruit every few days, then leaves, then only water, then only air, until by the fifth month he stands on one foot, holding the name, so still the worlds feel it. And Vishnu comes and stands before him. He gives Dhruva more than a seat on a lap: a place in the sky that never moves. Dhruva becomes the pole star, the one the others turn around. His name means fixed, firm. Patanjali's threads thirteen and fourteen describe what Dhruva did. Practice, abhyasa, is the effort to stay steady. Not the stillness; the effort, the coming back. And it becomes firm ground, dridha bhumi, when it's kept up for a long time, without break, and with devotion, satkara: care, reverence, as if it matters. That's the Hindu teaching on sadhana, daily practice: not intensity, but steadiness and devotion, over years. It's why someone's Nani can sit with the same name on the same mala every morning for decades. Most mornings feel ordinary. She keeps going anyway, with care. Patanjali never promises fireworks. He promises ground. And nobody's asking you to stand on one foot.

Repeat it softly with the breath, counting on your fingers if you like, the way a mala counts. When you drift, come back, and count the coming back as the practice, not the drifting as a failure. Nothing needs to happen; you're laying ground.
Abhyasa, practice, the effort to return. It becomes firm ground over a long time, steadily, with care, the way Dhruva became the star that doesn't move.
Your line: abhyasa, long, steady, with care, becomes firm ground. Dhruva, fixed. Three hundred days, and counting.

301.title: Nachiketa turns down Death's gifts
301.hook: Death offers a boy gold, horses, long life and heaven's music, and the boy says keep them
301.carry: vairagya: the wanting doesn't own you
301.tomorrow: three roads open: action, devotion, knowledge. which one first?
301.howItsDone: In Hindu teaching, vairagya is not only for monks: householders are taught to hold wealth, family and even religious rewards loosely, and the Yoga Sutras' opening chapter is often studied as a complete short course in meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, abhyasa: a long time, without break, with care, until it becomes firm ground. Dhruva, the star that doesn't move. Today, the other wing, and the week closes.

A boy named Nachiketa has waited three days at the door of Death. Yama, the lord of death, was away, and when he returns, ashamed to have left a guest hungry, he grants three wishes. For the third, Nachiketa asks the hardest thing: what happens after we die? Yama tries to buy him off. Take sons and grandsons who'll live a hundred years, he says. Cattle, elephants, gold, horses. Rule the earth. Live as long as you like. Take these heavenly women with their chariots and music; no mortal could win them. Just don't ask me that.
screen: `THREE DAYS AT DEATH'S DOOR.` → `WHAT HAPPENS AFTER WE DIE?` → `GOLD, HORSES, LONG LIFE, HEAVEN'S MUSIC.` → `JUST DON'T ASK.`

segments.voice: Nachiketa answers, in the Katha Upanishad: these won't last past tomorrow. Keep your horses, keep your songs. No one is made happy by wealth. And he holds out for the teaching, and that refusal is why Yama teaches him. That's vairagya, non-attachment, the second wing, and Patanjali's thread fifteen describes it: the mastery of one who no longer thirsts for things seen, or things heard about. Seen means this world: the praise, the paycheck, the last slice of cake. Heard about, says the commentary, includes heaven itself. Yama's heavenly music was exactly that, a reward you'd only heard of. Even spiritual prizes can become one more thing to crave. Patanjali's word for the result is vashikara: mastery, being in charge of the pull. Nachiketa didn't stop wanting. He wanted the truth more. Thread sixteen goes to the root: from knowing the seer comes freedom from thirst for everything nature is woven of. In Hindu teaching this isn't only for monks; householders are taught to hold money, success, even religious rewards loosely. Look back at the week: open hands for a teacher, a drunk monkey and a still lake, two birds, a self awake through sleep, two wings, a star that never moves, and a boy who said no thanks to Death.
screen: `THESE WON'T LAST PAST TOMORROW.` · `NO THIRST FOR THINGS SEEN OR HEARD OF.` · `VASHIKARA: MASTERY OF THE PULL.` · `HE WANTED THE TRUTH MORE.` · then, large: `TAT PARAṀ PURUṢA-KHYĀTER GUṆA-VAITṚṢṆYAM.`

segments.voice: Let one pull come to mind, something you've tasted and want again, or something you've only heard about and want anyway, and notice where you feel it: the chest, the stomach, the hands. Loosen your grip by one finger, then another; you don't have to give the thing up, only notice the wanting doesn't have to own you. If you pray, offer the wanting to God, the way many Hindus offer food before they eat it, so it comes back as prasad; if you don't, say quietly, i can enjoy this without it owning me.
Vairagya, non-attachment: mastery of the pull of what you've tasted and what you've only heard of. Nachiketa kept wanting one thing, the truth, and let the rest go.
Your line: vairagya, the wanting doesn't own you. Nachiketa said keep your horses. That's the week, and day three hundred one.
